gloss_terse: Balsam tree; a tree (possibly weeping or dripping with resin) in whose groves God directed Israel's military strategy.
gloss_readable: Refers to a specific species of tree, likely a balsam or mulberry, identified by its resinous dripping sap. The name may derive from a root meaning 'to weep' or 'to drip,' connecting it to the Arabic for a low-yield camel. In 2 Samuel 5:23-24 and 1 Chronicles 14:14-15, God instructs David to circle behind the Philistines through the balsam grove and wait for the sound of marching in the treetops as a divine signal to attack. Psalm 84:7 speaks of passing through the 'Valley of Baca,' a poetic image of turning a dry, weeping place into a spring of blessing.

senses.1: A balsam or mulberry tree, known for dripping resin, appearing only in the plural (בְּכָאִים). In 2 Samuel 5:23-24 and 1 Chronicles 14:14-15, God tells David to use a grove of these trees as tactical cover, with the rustling of their tops serving as the signal to advance. Spanish 'los-bálsamos' and English 'balsam-trees' both preserve the botanical identification. The singular form appears in Psalm 84:7's evocative 'Valley of Baca,' likely a parched place named for these weeping trees.

gloss_terse: To bear early fruit; to treat or designate as firstborn; to be in the pangs of a first birth.
gloss_readable: Covers a semantic range from agricultural earliness to the legal and physical dimensions of firstborn status. In the Piel stem, it means either to bear early or first fruit (Ezek 47:12) or to confer firstborn rights upon a son (Deut 21:16). The Pual indicates being born or designated as a firstling (Lev 27:26), while the Hiphil participle in Jeremiah 4:31 vividly describes a woman bearing her first child. The Arabic cognate بَكَرَ ('to rise early, do something early') illuminates the core notion of primacy and firstness that unifies these uses.

senses.1: To bear early or first fruit, to designate as firstborn, or to experience first childbirth. The Piel in Ezekiel 47:12 describes miraculous trees that 'bear early' every month. In Deuteronomy 21:16, a father may not 'make firstborn' a younger son over the actual firstborn — Spanish 'dar-primogenitura' and French 'est-fit-premier-né' capture this legal conferral. The Hiphil participle in Jeremiah 4:31 (מַבְכִּירָה) paints Zion as a woman in the anguish of her first delivery. The Pual in Leviticus 27:26 marks an animal 'made firstling' as already belonging to the LORD.

gloss_terse: To gleam, brighten up, smile; to cause a flash of destruction upon the strong.
gloss_readable: A rare verb found only in the Hiphil, carrying both the warmth of a brightened face and the violence of a sudden flash of ruin. In Job 9:27 and 10:20, Job resolves to set aside his complaint and 'brighten up' or 'show a smile,' an act of forced cheer in the face of suffering. Psalm 39:13 uses the same idiom as a plea: 'Look away from me, that I may smile again.' But Amos 5:9 turns the word ominous — God 'flashes destruction upon the stronghold,' the same gleam now wielded as judgment. The Arabic cognate بَلِجَ ('to gleam, be radiant') confirms the root image of sudden brightness.

senses.1: To show a gleam or smile, to look cheerful. Used in Job 9:27, 10:20, and Psalm 39:13, where the sufferer longs to 'brighten up' before death. Spanish 'me-alegraré' and German 'lass-mich-smile' both reflect this sense of forced or fleeting cheerfulness. In Amos 5:9, the same root takes a darker turn — God causes ruin to 'flash' or 'burst forth' upon the strong (המבליג שׁד על־עז), turning the image of radiant brightness into one of devastating judgment. French splits the nuance neatly: 'briller' for cheerfulness, 'briser' for destructive flashing.

gloss_terse: Bilhan; a personal name borne by a descendant of Esau and a Benjamite clan leader.
gloss_readable: A proper name appearing in genealogical lists. The first Bilhan is a Horite descendant of Esau listed among the clan chiefs of Seir in Genesis 36:27 and 1 Chronicles 1:42, placing him within Edom's pre-Israelite population. The second Bilhan is a son of Jediael in the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chr 7:10), a military leader whose family mustered thousands of warriors. The name is consistently transliterated across languages — English, Spanish, French, and German all render it 'Bilhan' — suggesting no competing etymological traditions.

senses.1: A personal name meaning possibly 'modest' or 'weak,' borne by two distinct individuals. The Horite Bilhan (Gen 36:27; 1 Chr 1:42) appears among Seir's indigenous clans absorbed into Edom. The Benjamite Bilhan (1 Chr 7:10) heads a family that produced 17,200 fighting men. All major translation traditions — Spanish 'Bilhán,' French 'Bilhan,' German 'Bilhan' — simply transliterate the name, confirming it functions as an opaque proper noun with no living semantic content in the target languages.

gloss_terse: Bamoth; a Moabite town on the heights, also called Bamoth-Baal, along Israel's wilderness route.
gloss_readable: A place name meaning 'high places,' referring to a town in Moab along the Israelites' journey toward the Promised Land. Numbers 21:19-20 lists it as a station between Nahaliel and the valley in the field of Moab. The fuller form Bamoth-Baal ('high places of Baal') in Numbers 22:41 identifies where Balak took Balaam to view and curse Israel — a cultic high place associated with Baal worship. Joshua 13:17 assigns it to the tribe of Reuben. The name's transparent meaning (from בָּמָה, 'high place') links geography, worship, and Israel's territorial claims.

senses.1: A Moabite settlement meaning 'high places,' stationed along Israel's wilderness itinerary (Num 21:19-20) and later assigned to Reuben (Josh 13:17). The expanded form Bamoth-Baal (Num 22:41) reveals its function as a Canaanite cultic site — Balak brought Balaam there to survey Israel from a vantage point sacred to Baal. Spanish 'Bamot-Baal,' French 'Bamoth-Baal,' and German 'Bamoth-Baal' all preserve both elements. The consistent transliteration across languages reflects its dual identity as both a geographic waypoint and a place of pagan worship.

gloss_terse: Son(s); used here in construct forms denoting kinship, membership, or belonging to a group or lineage.
gloss_readable: The extraordinarily common Hebrew word בֵּן ('son') appears here in a handful of construct or prepositional forms where it denotes lineage, group membership, or familial relationship. In Judges 20:13, 'sons of Belial' designates worthless men among the Benjamites. In 2 Kings 19:37 and Daniel 11:10, it marks a son in a literal dynastic succession. In 1 Chronicles 27:12, it identifies a military commander by his tribal or family affiliation. The word's flexibility — from literal offspring to metaphorical class membership — is reflected across all target languages.

senses.1: Son or sons in construct, marking kinship or group affiliation. This subset of occurrences uses the prepositional form לְבֵן or suffixed forms to express belonging — whether to a literal father (2 Kgs 19:37, where Sennacherib is struck down by 'his sons') or to a classification (Judg 20:13). Spanish renders variously as 'para-el-hijo,' 'sus-hijos,' while French uses 'et-fils' and German 'Söhne-von,' all reflecting the relational construct. In 1 Chronicles 27:12, it identifies a commander by descent, and in Daniel 11:10 it signals dynastic succession in prophetic vision.

gloss_terse: Unripe or sour grapes; used both literally of premature fruit and proverbially of inherited guilt.
gloss_readable: Denotes grapes that are not yet ripe — either green and hard or sour and astringent. Isaiah 18:5 uses it literally: God will cut away vine branches when the blossom becomes a ripening grape, just before harvest. Job 15:33 compares the wicked to a vine that shakes off its unripe grapes prematurely. But the word is best known from the proverb quoted in Jeremiah 31:29 and Ezekiel 18:2: 'The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge' — a complaint about inherited punishment that both prophets then overturn with the principle of individual responsibility.

senses.1: Unripe or sour grapes, used of fruit that has not reached maturity and carries an unpleasant taste. In Isaiah 18:5, it appears in an agricultural metaphor for God's pre-harvest pruning of nations. Job 15:33 compares the wicked to an olive tree casting off its blossoms and a vine dropping its unripe grapes (בִּסְרוֹ). The proverbial use in Jeremiah 31:29-30 and Ezekiel 18:2 — Spanish 'uvas-agrias,' English 'sour-grapes' — embeds the word in a theological argument: the old saying about fathers eating sour grapes and children suffering is declared obsolete. The Arabic cognate بُسْر ('unripe dates') confirms the core sense of premature, unpalatable fruit.

gloss_terse: Baal (II); a place name in Simeon and a personal name for a Reubenite and two Gibeonites.
gloss_readable: Distinguished from the deity name Baal, this homograph functions as both a place name and a personal name. As a place, it designates a city in the tribal territory of Simeon (1 Chr 4:33), identified with Baalath-Beer elsewhere. As a personal name, it is borne by a Reubenite (1 Chr 5:5), and by a Gibeonite ancestor of Saul listed in 1 Chronicles 8:30 and 9:36. The name's association with the Canaanite deity is incidental here — these are simply individuals and a town bearing a once-common Semitic name meaning 'lord' or 'master.'

senses.1: A proper noun — either a Simeonite town (1 Chr 4:33, equivalent to Baalath-Beer) or a personal name borne by a Reubenite (1 Chr 5:5) and a Gibeonite (1 Chr 8:30; 9:36). French and German render it in brackets ([בעל]) as a transliteration, while Spanish and English use 'Baal' directly. Unlike the deity Baal worshipped by Canaanites, this homograph functions purely as a geographic or genealogical identifier, though both derive from the common Semitic root meaning 'lord, master, owner.'

gloss_terse: Mistress, female owner; a woman who possesses or is characterized by something — a household, sorcery, or necromancy.
gloss_readable: The feminine counterpart of בַּעַל ('master, owner'), used to describe a woman defined by what she possesses or practices. In 1 Kings 17:17, the 'mistress of the house' (בַּעֲלַת הַבַּיִת) is the widow of Zarephath who hosted Elijah — a dignified title of domestic authority. In 1 Samuel 28:7, the same construction identifies the famous 'mistress of a spirit' (בַּעֲלַת אוֹב), the medium at Endor whom Saul consulted. Nahum 3:4 applies it to Nineveh as 'mistress of sorceries' (בַּעֲלַת כְשָׁפִים), personifying the city as a seductive enchantress.

senses.1: A woman who owns, possesses, or is characterized by a particular domain or skill. The construct בַּעֲלַת ('mistress of') links to a following noun to define the relationship: 'mistress of the house' in 1 Kings 17:17 (French 'maîtresse,' Spanish 'dueña-de'), 'mistress of a necromantic spirit' at Endor (1 Sam 28:7), and 'mistress of sorceries' describing Nineveh's seductive power (Nah 3:4). German 'mistress-von' and English 'mistress-of' both preserve the possessive construct. The word dignifies the woman's authority over her sphere — whether a household, a forbidden craft, or an empire's dark allure.

gloss_terse: Baal-Zebub; the deity of Ekron whose name means 'lord of the flies,' consulted by King Ahaziah.
gloss_readable: A compound divine name meaning 'lord of the flies,' designating the Philistine deity worshipped at Ekron. All four occurrences appear in 2 Kings 1:2-16, where King Ahaziah of Israel, after falling through a lattice, sends messengers to inquire of Baal-Zebub whether he will recover. Elijah intercepts them with a stinging rebuke: 'Is it because there is no God in Israel that you go to inquire of Baal-Zebub?' The name may be a deliberate Hebrew distortion of an original 'Baal-Zebul' ('lord of the exalted dwelling'), turned into 'lord of flies' as a polemical insult against the foreign god.

senses.1: The Philistine deity of Ekron, 'lord of the flies' (בַּעַל זְבוּב), consulted by the injured King Ahaziah in 2 Kings 1:2, 3, 6, 16. Every translation tradition preserves the compound name: Spanish 'Baal-zebub,' French 'Baal-Zebub,' German 'Baal-Zebub,' English 'Baal-Zebub.' The prepositional form (לבעל זבוב, 'to Baal-Zebub') marks Ahaziah's act of seeking an oracle from a foreign god rather than from the LORD — the central offense that Elijah denounces. Scholars suspect the original name was Baal-Zebul ('lord of the exalted place'), deliberately corrupted by Hebrew writers to the derisive 'lord of flies.'
